summary: The paper addresses an important HCI problem: how to design AI agents that are both helpful and safe in interactive environments. The user studies are well-designed and provide valuable insights into user perceptions of safety and control.
strengths: Good use of both between-subjects and within-subjects designs
Clear measurement of both objective performance and subjective experience
Thoughtful discussion of the trade-off between safety and utility
Well-motivated design choices based on user needs
weaknesses: Limited demographic information about study participants
No exploration of individual differences in response to the system
The approval workflow interface could be described in more detail
Missing discussion of learnability - how users' behavior changes over time
Could benefit from qualitative feedback from users about their experience
questions: How long did it take users to become comfortable with the approval workflow?
Did users develop any workarounds or strategies to minimize approval overhead?
Were there any differences in how different user groups (e.g., moderators vs regular members) responded to the system?
How did users perceive the proactive suggestions - as helpful or intrusive?
What was the approval rate for different types of suggested actions?
missing_references: Work on trust calibration in human-AI interaction
Studies on notification timing and user interruption costs
Research on explainable AI and user understanding of system behavior
